On the third Thursday of every month, the committee met in the back room of the library, and the meeting always began the same way: a pot of coffee that nobody drank, a stack of minutes from the previous month, and a long silence while the chair shuffled her papers. The agenda rarely changed. There was the matter of the leaking roof, which had been discussed for eleven years and repaired twice; the question of whether to plant bulbs along the eastern path (approved, deferred, approved again); and the recurring complaint about the noise from the ferry terminal, which everyone agreed was getting worse and no one could prove. Outside, the tide came in and went out, indifferent to the proceedings, and the gulls argued on the pilings as if they too had business to settle. When the clock above the door struck nine, the treasurer would clear his throat, unfold his glasses, and read the balance in a voice so quiet that the others leaned forward together, like a field of wheat bending before the same wind.

Nobody ever remembered afterward what the numbers were. What they remembered was the walk home, the salt in the air, the lights of the boats swinging at anchor, and the certainty, vague but durable, that the town was still there and that its small rituals held it together better than any budget could. The library itself had been built in 1908 with money from a mill owner whose name no longer appeared on any plaque, and the reading room still kept his portrait above the fireplace, a stern man in a dark coat holding a book he had probably never opened. Children did their homework at the long oak tables; retired fishermen read the same pages of the same newspaper twice; and in winter, when the wind came off the water hard enough to rattle the windows, the librarian would make tea for anyone who stayed past closing time, which was against the rules and happened anyway.

By the time the meeting ended, the streets were dark and the shops had closed, and the committee members walked out under the streetlamps in twos and threes, still arguing quietly about the roof or the bulbs or the ferry, though none of the arguments would change anything before spring. This was not a failure, the chair liked to say; it was simply how things were done in a place where everyone knew everyone else and no decision could be made without somebody's grandmother being consulted first. The system was slow, and it was stubborn, and it occasionally produced results so sensible that visitors from the city went home wondering why their own councils could not manage the same. On the whole, the town considered itself lucky, and it was, though not for the reasons it usually gave.
